quests.instruction: Find the first place where one word runs into the next
quests.textToSpeak: we'd like to extend our stay by two nights if possible
quests.hint: The earliest link sits near the front of the sentence. Which pair?
quests.explanation: Hotel requests are polite and fluid. The /nd/ of 'extend' is carried into the vowel of 'our'. The second link, 'nights if', follows.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link is carried by a buzz or a hiss?
quests.textToSpeak: is the hotel within walking distance of the main square
quests.hint: Which link is carried by a hiss?
quests.explanation: Directions and distances are said quickly. The /s/ of 'distance' runs into the weak /əv/ of 'of', and the stress then falls on 'main square'. Nothing else in the sentence joins a consonant to a vowel.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by the sound /l/
quests.textToSpeak: they said there'd be a shuttle at ten but nobody turned up
quests.hint: Say 'lll' at the end of each word in turn. Which one runs on into a vowel?
quests.explanation: A traveller reporting a no-show says this in a rush. The syllabic /l/ of 'shuttle' runs into the weak /æt/ of 'at'. 'Turned up' links through /d/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Find the link that runs on a hum (m, n or ng)
quests.textToSpeak: I can do Tuesday morning or Wednesday afternoon whichever suits you
quests.hint: Hum through the sentence slowly. At one boundary the hum rolls straight into a vowel.
quests.explanation: Scheduling talk is said quickly. The /ŋ/ of 'morning' runs into the weak /ɔː/ of 'or', so the options sound like two beats. 'Wednesday afternoon' joins two vowels with a light /j/, a different link.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which connection comes first in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: we have to reschedule because something urgent has come up
quests.hint: Ignore everything after the first link you hear.
quests.explanation: Apologising for a reschedule is done in one breath. The /ŋ/ of 'something' runs into the vowel of 'urgent', so the phrase lands as one unit. 'Come up' follows through /m/.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Spot the vowel-to-vowel link that takes a 'y' glide
quests.textToSpeak: could we push it back by about twenty minutes
quests.hint: The first word ends in a sound like 'ee', 'ay' or 'eye'. What comes next?
quests.explanation: A friendly request to shift a time is said smoothly. 'By' ends in /aɪ/ and 'about' begins with /ə/, so a light /j/ eases across. 'Push it' links through /ʃ/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which pair changes into a 'ch', 'j' or 'sh' sound when said quickly?
quests.textToSpeak: I'm so sorry for the inconvenience and I appreciate your patience
quests.hint: In casual speech a final consonant and a 'y' sound at the start of the next word blend. Which pair?
quests.explanation: 'Appreciate your' becomes 'appreciatcher' as /t/ and /j/ fuse into /tʃ/. In an apology, a careful speaker may keep the sounds apart to sound formal; both are correct.
quests.flowRule: Yod-coalescence (informal speech): When a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ is followed by 'you' or 'your', the two sounds often merge into one: /t/+/j/ becomes /tʃ/ ('got you' sounds like 'gotcha'), /d/+/j/ becomes /dʒ/ ('did you' like 'didja'), /s/+/j/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/+/j/ becomes /ʒ/. This is a normal informal reduction, not a mistake, and careful speakers may keep the sounds apart.

quests.instruction: Which word-final r connects to the next vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: thanks so much for all your help it made a real difference
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in 'or' before a vowel.
quests.explanation: Non-rhotic speakers bring the /r/ of 'for' back before a vowel, and rhotic speakers say it every time, so 'for all' sounds like one beat. 'Made a' links through /d/.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Which link has a light /w/ glide between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: I really owe you an apology for the way I spoke earlier
quests.hint: Two vowel sounds touch with no consonant between. After rounded lips, listen for a faint 'w'.
quests.explanation: A faint /w/ eases across after the /uː/ of 'you' into the weak vowel of 'an'. 'Way I' and 'really owe' join vowels too, but after /eɪ/ and /i/, which call for /j/. 'An apology' links through /n/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /w/ glide: After vowels made with rounded lips (/uː/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/), many speakers slide through a light /w/ before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a 'ch' or 'j' sound?
quests.textToSpeak: let's keep in touch and arrange something for next month
quests.hint: Find the word whose last sound is like the start of 'church' or 'judge'. What follows it?
quests.explanation: The 'ch' of 'touch' is released into the weak /ən/ of 'and', so the farewell is one smooth phrase. 'Keep in' and 'and arrange' link through other sounds.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Find the link that slides through a 'w' sound
quests.textToSpeak: safe travels and let me know when you arrive
quests.hint: Say each candidate slowly. A light /w/ appears between two vowels only once.
quests.explanation: A farewell is said warmly and smoothly. 'You' ends in /uː/ and 'arrive' begins with the weak /ə/, so a light /w/ eases between them. 'Travels and' links through /z/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /w/ glide: After vowels made with rounded lips (/uː/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/), many speakers slide through a light /w/ before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which is the last connection in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: I'll post the photos as soon as I've sorted them out
quests.hint: Count the joins from the left and take the highest number.
quests.explanation: Social messages are said casually. The /m/ of 'them' runs into the /aʊ/ of 'out', so 'sorted them out' ends as one chunk. 'As soon as' and its neighbours link earlier.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which connection of any kind comes first?
quests.textToSpeak: if you're free on Saturday we could grab a coffee and chat
quests.hint: The first place where one word runs into the next is the target.
quests.explanation: After the /iː/ of 'free', a light /j/ eases across into the vowel of 'on'. 'Grab a' and 'coffee and' follow in the same relaxed rhythm of an invitation.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which pair merges into a new sound in casual speech?
quests.textToSpeak: I should arrive at your place around ten
quests.hint: Say the candidates slowly, then fast. Which pair turns into a new sound when fast?
quests.explanation: 'At your' becomes 'atcher' as /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/. 'Arrive at' and 'place around' link through /v/ and /s/. A text about arrival plans is written and spoken in this relaxed way.
quests.flowRule: Yod-coalescence (informal speech): When a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ is followed by 'you' or 'your', the two sounds often merge into one: /t/+/j/ becomes /tʃ/ ('got you' sounds like 'gotcha'), /d/+/j/ becomes /dʒ/ ('did you' like 'didja'), /s/+/j/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/+/j/ becomes /ʒ/. This is a normal informal reduction, not a mistake, and careful speakers may keep the sounds apart.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a written r returns before a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: I'd love to hear all about it afterwards
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in a written r before a vowel.
quests.explanation: In most accents, the written r of 'hear' is pronounced when a vowel follows, so the /r/ links into the vowel of 'all'. 'All about', 'about it' and 'it afterwards' follow, so the sentence is a chain from 'hear' to the end.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Which pair links even though the first word ends in a silent e?
quests.textToSpeak: please leave it at reception and I'll collect it later
quests.hint: Say the first word of the pair without thinking about its spelling.
quests.explanation: 'Leave' is spelled with a final e, but it ends in /v/, which runs into 'it'. The silent letter plays no role. In a long sentence like this, the first link is easiest to recognise because the rest follows at speed.
quests.flowRule: Linking follows sound, not spelling: a silent final 'e' (as in 'give' or 'close') does not block a link, because the word really ends in a consonant sound such as /v/ or /z/.

quests.instruction: Which link goes into a word with a silent h?
quests.textToSpeak: she's an heir to a large fortune
quests.hint: One word begins with a letter you do not pronounce.
quests.explanation: The h of 'heir' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel and takes 'an', which links straight in. 'She's an' links through /z/ in the same sentence.
quests.flowRule: Silent 'h': In words like 'hour', 'honest' and 'honour' the written h is not pronounced, so the word begins with a vowel sound and links to the word before it (and takes 'an', not 'a').

quests.instruction: Spot the spelling trap: which pair has no real vowel link?
quests.textToSpeak: that's a useless piece of software
quests.hint: Spelling can suggest two vowels in a row. Which pair does not actually have two vowel sounds meeting?
quests.explanation: 'Useless' begins with /j/, so nothing links between 'a' and 'useless'. The real links in this sentence are 'that's a' and 'piece of'.
quests.flowRule: Sound, not spelling (glides): Spelling can suggest a vowel-to-vowel link where there is none. 'One' begins with /w/ and 'unique' with /j/, so they are consonant sounds. Check the first sound of a word, not its first letter.

quests.instruction: Where does a faint 'w' appear between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: the blue ink is running low
quests.hint: The first word ends with the lips rounded, like 'oo', 'oh' or 'ow'. What comes next?
quests.explanation: A faint /w/ eases between the /uː/ of 'blue' and the /ɪ/ of 'ink'. 'Ink is' links through /k/, a stop, so the two links differ in kind.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /w/ glide: After vowels made with rounded lips (/uː/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/), many speakers slide through a light /w/ before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a linking /r/?
quests.textToSpeak: my brother and I are planning a trip in August
quests.hint: Which word's last letter is r, with a vowel right after it?
quests.explanation: Only one link here carries a linking r: the written r of 'brother' appears before the weak /ən/ of 'and' in most accents. 'And I', 'trip in' and others link in other ways.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Where might some speakers add an /r/ that is not in the spelling?
quests.textToSpeak: this area of the city is quiet
quests.hint: A word ends in a weak or open vowel with no r in its spelling, and another vowel follows. Which pair?
quests.explanation: Some non-rhotic speakers say 'arear of', adding an /r/ although none is written. Others glide or pause slightly. It is accent-dependent: recognise it, but you need not produce it.
quests.flowRule: Intrusive /r/ (accent-dependent): In some non-rhotic accents speakers add an /r/ between a word ending in /ə/, /ɑː/ or /ɔː/ and a following vowel even when no r is written (idea of sounds like 'idear of'). It is common in those accents and absent in others, so it is useful to recognise but not something you need to produce.

quests.instruction: Where do two sounds blend into one in fast, informal speech?
quests.textToSpeak: I want you to know that I really value your help
quests.hint: A final /t/ or /d/ can melt into a following 'y' sound. Where?
quests.explanation: 'Want you' becomes 'wantcha' as /t/ and /j/ fuse into /tʃ/. A heartfelt line is often said this way, so the merge sounds friendly rather than careless.
quests.flowRule: Yod-coalescence (informal speech): When a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ is followed by 'you' or 'your', the two sounds often merge into one: /t/+/j/ becomes /tʃ/ ('got you' sounds like 'gotcha'), /d/+/j/ becomes /dʒ/ ('did you' like 'didja'), /s/+/j/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/+/j/ becomes /ʒ/. This is a normal informal reduction, not a mistake, and careful speakers may keep the sounds apart.

quests.instruction: Which pair's first word changes its last sound to match the next sound?
quests.textToSpeak: we've been in meetings all morning
quests.hint: A nasal meets a lip sound. What does it do?
quests.explanation: Before /m/ the /n/ of 'in' often becomes /m/, giving 'im meetings'. 'Been in' and 'meetings all' link through /n/ and /ŋz/ instead. The shift is easy to miss because it is so small.
quests.flowRule: Place assimilation (informal speech): At the end of a word, /t/, /d/ and /n/ often take on the place of the next sound. Before /p b m/ they shift towards lip sounds (ten people sounds like 'tem people'; bad back like 'bab back'), and before /k g/ towards back-of-the-mouth sounds (in case like 'ing case'). It is common in fast speech and listeners barely notice it.

quests.instruction: Which pair loses a consonant in fast, casual speech?
quests.textToSpeak: the best moment is seeing everyone together
quests.hint: Find the pair that loses a consonant in fast speech.
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'best' is often dropped before /m/, so you hear 'bes moment'. The rest of the sentence uses links such as 'seeing everyone', which are different in kind.
quests.flowRule: Elision (informal speech): A /t/ or /d/ between two other consonants is often left out in fast speech, so 'next day' sounds like 'nex day' and 'old man' like 'ol man'. The words still connect smoothly; the consonant cluster simply gets lighter.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a consonant cluster?
quests.textToSpeak: she walked out of the meeting and slammed the door
quests.hint: The last sound of the cluster joins the vowel. Which word has such an ending?
quests.explanation: The dramatic verb-plus-particle is one beat: the /kt/ of 'walked' hands its /t/ to the /aʊ/ of 'out'. 'Out of' and 'meeting and' link through single consonants.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which link carries the past-tense ending?
quests.textToSpeak: the committee approved it unanimously and everyone was relieved
quests.hint: Past-tense endings often sound like /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/. Which one meets a vowel?
quests.explanation: The /d/ of 'approved' (/vd/) lands on the vowel of 'it', so the past tense stays audible. 'Unanimously and' joins two vowels with a light /j/, and 'and everyone' links through /d/.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which link closes the sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: it takes a lot of practice but it gets easier
quests.hint: After the final link, nothing else in the sentence connects. Where is it?
quests.explanation: Encouragement ends as one flowing phrase: the /ts/ of 'gets' lands on the /iː/ of 'easier'. 'Takes a', 'lot of' and 'but it' come earlier, each a small word on the end of a bigger one.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link has a light /j/ ('y') glide between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: thank you so much for helping me out
quests.hint: Mouth in a smile, then straight into a new vowel. Where?
quests.explanation: A thank-you like this is said warmly and fast. A light /j/ slips between the /iː/ of 'me' and the /aʊ/ of 'out'. 'For helping' and 'helping me' do not link, so only this pair joins two vowels.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a word ending in two consonants joins a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: I honestly think you handled it better than I would have
quests.hint: Which link ends in a heavier consonant group than the others?
quests.explanation: The /ld/ of 'handled' hands its /d/ to the vowel of 'it', so the compliment flows. 'I honestly' joins two vowels with a light /j/, a different kind of link. Capstone sentences blend several link types, so name each one as you hear it.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which word-final r connects to the next vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: I'd rather you hear it from me than from anyone else
quests.hint: Some accents say the r every time and some only before a vowel. Where does a vowel follow an r-word?
quests.explanation: Rhotic speakers always make this link and non-rhotic speakers add the /r/ before a vowel: the final /r/ of 'hear' runs into 'it'. 'From me' does not link, while 'from anyone' and 'anyone else' do, through /m/ and /n/.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.
